lines: A small catalog built from scratch just proved every real job a catalog needs to do actually works.
But proving an idea once isn't the same as everyone agreeing on how to talk to it.
This step builds the real, shared protocol that lets any engine speak to any catalog, over real HTTP, right here.
Picture a brand-new client meeting this catalog for the very first time.
It already has some config of its own, assumptions about where things live and how to behave.
Does it just start firing off requests using those assumptions, or does something have to happen before any of that?
answer: Think about what could go wrong if the client just guessed.
Its own assumptions might not match what this particular server actually expects or where it actually wants things stored.

lines: Something happens first, and it's a real call with a real answer.
The client asks for configuration, and the server hands back values the client has to layer onto its own.
Its own defaults come first, then whatever the client already set, and the server's own overrides win last, replacing anything underneath them.
With that settled, a real load works exactly the way any query engine would expect, fetching a table's current state over the wire.
Then the interesting part: two engines read that same table at the same moment and both try to commit.
Each one states, as part of its own request, the exact state it saw when it read -- a real condition the server has to check.
Here's the sharper question.
Time passes, and one of those two engines' stated condition no longer matches what the server actually holds.
Does the server just go ahead and accept that commit anyway, or does it refuse it?
answer: If the server accepted it anyway, two engines could silently stomp on each other's changes.
A protocol serious about correctness has to check that condition and refuse the commit when it no longer holds.

lines: It refuses it, and it tells you exactly why.
The losing engine gets back a real rejection naming the precise condition that no longer matched, not some generic failure.
So it reloads the table, sees the real current state, and retries -- this time it succeeds.
Now, a handful of real protocol features this script doesn't build, only names and sources honestly.
One lets several tables commit together as a single atomic step, instead of one table at a time.
Two more endpoints exist for registering an already-written table and for listing an entirely separate kind of object the protocol supports, called a view.
One more real feature, named precisely rather than faked: how a client gets temporary access to the actual storage underneath a table.
The client signals which mechanisms it can handle, and the server decides whether to hand any of them back.
This sandbox genuinely can't issue real temporary cloud access, so this piece stays sourced, not built.
Two more pieces worth naming before we close this out.
Newer catalogs can now plan a scan on the server's own side instead of leaving every engine to work it out alone, and the protocol has its own format for sharing reusable functions across engines.
Meanwhile the protocol's own original way of handing out login tokens is being phased out, in favor of letting a dedicated identity system handle that instead.
So here's where this leaves things.
A real catalog, speaking a real slice of the real shared protocol -- negotiating its config, loading a table, and committing with a condition the server actually checks.
Every mechanism this whole section needed now genuinely exists, built or carefully sourced.
What's left isn't a new mechanism at all. It's the practical choice every one of these pieces was really in service of: which format, and which catalog, do you actually reach for?
